jurisdictions.name: Karnataka
jurisdictions.verified: ECI annexure; dates are original, and may be superseded
jurisdictions.tag: What an objection can—and cannot—establish
jurisdictions.deck: Bulk Form 7 applications are a legitimate object of forensic examination. Their existence alone does not prove that voters were deleted or that crimes were committed.
jurisdictions.lead: Karnataka presents a test of two systems operating in parallel: electoral adjudication and criminal investigation. In October 2026, proceedings concerning allegedly false Form 7 objections were reported in the High Court. The central evidence is the original application, applicant authentication, the objected-to elector’s response, and what the ERO actually decided.
story: Applications are not deletions

An applicant may claim that a registered person died, shifted, duplicated an entry or lacked eligibility. The ERO must consider the statutory ground and the evidence. An unproved assertion in Form 7 should not be counted as a completed deletion.
A historical warning

The Commission’s account of the Aland matter described 6,018 applications in 2023, of which 24 were considered genuine. That historical incident is an important comparator—but not proof about people involved in 2026 litigation.
Electronic provenance matters
Preservation should reach original forms, submission timestamps, authentication events and case histories. A headline about a stay or alleged impersonation is not a signed criminal judgment.
questions: Can authenticated High Court orders and case numbers be obtained?
How many disputed objections were accepted, rejected or left pending?
What do original electronic submission records show?

jurisdictions.name: Maharashtra
jurisdictions.verified: ECI annexure; dates are original, and may be superseded
jurisdictions.tag: A moving deadline, and a data-quality question
jurisdictions.deck: Maharashtra brings two distinct issues into focus: changing public deadlines and an alleged birth-year anomaly in the underlying data.
jurisdictions.lead: The signed 12 October ECI extension now establishes Maharashtra’s revised timetable. The 9 October CEO bulletin separately records application intake. Neither source settles actual registration outcomes.
story: The timetable must have one authoritative version

Original ECI Annexure VI envisaged an October 7 final roll. Later instructions superseded that schedule. Before advising any applicant, the latest signed order and the required notification must be checked; a cached district page does not settle the matter.
A data error is not automatically a deletion

Reporting described approximately 2.7 lakh anomalous ages, concentrated in some Nashik constituencies. The meaningful question is not just whether the data were corrected, but whether incorrect values triggered unnecessary notices or changed any ERO decision.
What would establish impact
A complete incident report would connect each affected record to its source value, ETL transformations, notice history, corrected value and final registration status.
questions: Locate the actual State Gazette issue publishing the 12 October notification; the signed notification itself has now been obtained.
Were any decisions affected by the alleged 1900 birth-year defaults?
Can ERO decisions be reconciled with final roll supplements?

jurisdictions.name: NCT of Delhi
jurisdictions.verified: ECI annexure; dates are original, and may be superseded
jurisdictions.tag: A large verification exercise under a changing timetable
jurisdictions.deck: A Delhi court order records a route back through Form 6. Whether the applications became entries on the roll remains a separate question.
jurisdictions.lead: Delhi’s timetable changed more than once. Signed July and August orders establish earlier targets. Later September directions and the 17 October CEO press note identify the extended claims period. The note also reports Form 6 intake, which is not a count of completed registrations.
story: The baseline is a reference, not a verdict
Being unlinked to the January 2002 roll is not proof of non-citizenship or absence of ordinary residence in 2026. The legal question for the ERO remains present eligibility.
The response to a notice must count

The number of people who supplied documents is an activity measure. What matters for inclusion is how many decisions were made, how many were favourable and whether the correct entries appeared in the final roll.
A practical route to accountability
Data should be obtainable by constituency: flagged cases, served notices, responses received, reasons for rejection, successful appeals and corrections.
What the 14 October order records

In W.P.(C) 14955/2026, the Court closed the writ proceedings and allowed the two petitioners to fill Form 6 for processing under law. This records an application route, not a completed restoration or a ruling on every challenged declaration.
The date on the page and the date on the order

The district directory lists the revised schedule under 19 September, but the signed letter itself is dated 19 August. It sets a 31 August draft and earlier September/November targets. Later extensions must be read separately.
Applications received are not names restored

The 17 October CEO note’s indexed text reports 232,514 Form 6 applications during the claims period and 212,400 before draft publication. These are intake counts. Acceptance, unique people and published inclusion are not established by those totals.
The qualifying date in the July bundle

The CEO forwarding letter refers to 1 October, while the attached ECI order’s subject refers to 1 July. The timetable dates match. This is a wording inconsistency, not proof of an incorrect eligibility decision. The later August order uses 1 October.
questions: How many discrepancy notices were disposed of before the final roll?
How many eligible electors were successfully restored following follow-up visits?
Were all claims-period extensions reflected in accessible official notices?

story: What the controlling order says
Annexure VI of the 14 May 2026 order provides an internally consistent schedule. Any later amendment should be examined separately.
Why the correction stays public
A research archive should preserve its corrections. The evidence label was changed when the original document was examined, rather than concealing the old error.
What remains worth investigating
The further question is whether actual revision steps, notifications, Form 6 submissions and decision registers followed the operative schedule.

jurisdictions.verified: ECI annexure; dates are original, and may be superseded
jurisdictions.tag: From an original date anomaly to a reconciled final roll
jurisdictions.deck: A later operational bulletin narrows the printed-date question. The October final report supplies a district-level reconciliation.
jurisdictions.lead: The May annexure’s 10 July notice start is a historical printed-date discrepancy. The July operational bulletin instead begins that window on 14 July. The final report published on 3 October now gives a stronger basis for analysing aggregate outcomes.
story: Narrow the earlier question

The operational bulletin starts the notice/disposal window on 14 July. This does not prove whether any individual notice was served earlier, but it removes any basis to describe the May date alone as proof of actual pre-draft proceedings.
The arithmetic now has a primary source

Case files, notice-service evidence, reasons, appeals and publication dates are still required to decide the correctness of individual exclusions.
questions: Were any notices actually issued before the draft, despite the July operational window?

jurisdictions.name: Bihar
jurisdictions.group: Other states and UTs in Annexure V
jurisdictions.verified: Reference-roll record, not a statement of current SIR completion
jurisdictions.tag: The case that reached the Supreme Court
jurisdictions.deck: Bihar supplies the constitutional judgment, but the difference between a lawful process and a correct individual decision remains central to the record.
jurisdictions.lead: A contested enumeration campaign in 2025 changed the language of India’s electoral-roll debate. Its draft was missing roughly 65 lakh entries from the pre-revision electorate. Months later, the Supreme Court upheld the Commission’s authority and the framework used. Neither event, alone, tells us whether every omitted citizen had a fair chance to remain on the roll.
story: What the Court decided

In May 2026 the Supreme Court held that Article 324 and Section 21(3) allow special intensive revision. The Court accepted the central aim of correcting the register and found the Bihar framework compliant with the governing election rules. It maintained a boundary: an ERO’s inquiry into eligibility must not be mistaken for formal adjudication of Indian citizenship.
What the numbers leave unanswered

A draft name not found and a final deletion are different events. The official figures record approximately 21.53 lakh additions and 3.66 lakh further removals between draft and final. Without identity-level links, a simple subtraction cannot identify how many people from the original missing cohort later returned.
Where scrutiny belongs
For any challenged case, the source is a specific ERO order: the alleged ground, BLO inquiries, the notice and the hearing record. A system-wide judgment cannot substitute for inspecting those files.
questions: How many of the draft’s 65 lakh absent names reappeared through Form 6 or corrections?
What evidence supported the combined “shifted/not found” classification?
Were appeals and citizenship referrals resolved within the prescribed periods?

jurisdictions.deck: In Goa, the state CEO’s own report permits a proper accounting of the change from the old roll to the final register. It also points to thousands of decisions still requiring individual audit.
jurisdictions.lead: The Goa case is not principally about one dramatic number. It is about whether each part of the roll can be explained. The state’s signed final-publication report separates draft omissions, accepted additions, form-based deletions and determinations made after discrepancy proceedings. It provides the clearest opportunity yet to connect software flags to accountable decisions.
story: A reconciliation that balances

Starting from the draft, 12,166 accepted additions and 39,592 removals produce the reported final electorate exactly. Of those removals, 3,812 were processed through forms, while 35,780 followed eligibility proceedings relating to unmatched records or logical discrepancies.
The flags behind the notices

ECINet reportedly flagged 58,923 logical discrepancies among historically linked voters; 41,116 involved a father’s-name mismatch. Names can differ through spelling, transliteration or source error. A flag is a request for examination, not proof that an elector is ineligible.
The unfinished 97-person file

The September account recorded 81 submitted applications. Later PTI reporting recorded 88 accepted applications. Neither figure is this publication’s inspection of the individual orders and restored roll entries.
questions: What statutory grounds supported each of the 35,780 post-draft eligibility decisions?
Of the 97 persons, how many are now enrolled and by which process?
Which ECINet matching-rule versions were used, and could authorised ERO decisions be implemented?

jurisdictions.tag: Judicial safeguards in practice
jurisdictions.deck: The West Bengal proceedings illustrate how the courts can order exceptional procedures without rewriting the system for the entire country.
jurisdictions.lead: In West Bengal, the question moved from whether a revision could happen to whether affected electors could understand and challenge discrepancies. Supreme Court orders in January and February 2026 addressed notice accessibility and the adjudication of pending cases, including an exceptional role for judicial officers.
story: Notice that can be acted upon

The January order directs accessible lists, authorised representatives and additional time linked to list display. These are judicial safeguards; implementation still needs dated registers and receipt records.
Exceptional does not mean universal

The February order invokes Article 142 for an extraordinary West Bengal arrangement involving judicial officers. Its paragraph 9 also permits an ongoing process and later supplementary lists. This is not a universal replacement of ERO duties.
The missing denominator
Without full sets of notices, decisions, successful challenges and appeals, it is impossible to measure accurately how many eligible electors were finally and wrongly excluded.
